Red Flags. Green Flags. One Goal: Protecting the Financial Ecosystem.

Fraud detection is not simply about identifying a suspicious transaction. It is about understanding behaviour, connecting patterns, and making informed decisions before financial harm occurs.

🚩 Red Flags may include:
• Unusual transaction patterns
• Sudden changes in customer behaviour
• Multiple failed authentication attempts
• Suspicious device or login activity
• Inconsistencies in customer information

🟢 Green Flags can include:
• Consistent transaction behaviour
• Verified customer information
• Trusted devices and authentication
• Expected spending patterns
• Behaviour aligned with the customer's profile

But why does this matter?

Fraud doesn't impact just one transaction—or even one customer. It can result in financial losses, identity theft, customer distrust, regulatory exposure, and reputational damage. At scale, persistent financial crime can undermine confidence in financial institutions and the broader financial system.

That's why effective fraud detection requires more than rules and alerts. It requires analytical thinking, continuous monitoring, strong controls, and the ability to distinguish genuine anomalies from legitimate customer behaviour.

The real skill isn't just spotting the red flag. It's understanding what happened before it—and what could happen next.

In fraud prevention, every transaction tells a story. The challenge is learning to read it.

#Fraud Classification of Cash Shortages: RBI Reporting Norms Explained in line with RBI's Master Directions on Fraud Risk Management.

Cash Shortages – When to Treat as Fraud

1. Cash shortage of ₹10,000 and above

Any cash shortage of ₹10,000 or more should be reported immediately as suspected Fraud, irrespective of whether fraudulent intent has been established at that stage. This is because of the seriousness of such shortages and the need for prompt reporting and investigation before fraud gets actually established.


2. Cash shortage between ₹5,000 and ₹10,000

Such cases are treated as fraud only if all the following conditions are satisfied:

The shortage is detected by management, an auditor, or an inspecting officer.

The person handling the cash did not report the shortage on the day it occurred.

Fraudulent intention is suspected or established at the time of detection.


3. Negligence

Mere negligence does not constitute fraud.

However, where negligence is accompanied by dishonest intention, misappropriation, concealment or intent to cheat/defraud, the case should be classified and reported as a fraud.


Takeaways for bankers

# ₹10,000 or more cash shortage: Report as fraud immediately and initiate investigation.

# ₹5,000–₹10,000 shortage: Examine whether it was promptly reported and whether there is evidence or suspicion of fraudulent intent before classifying it as fraud.

#Negligence alone: Deal with it as a disciplinary or operational lapse unless evidence indicates fraudulent intent.

Fraud is determined not just by the amount involved but also by the presence of dishonest intention.

A finance team approves a supplier invoice that looks legitimate. Money transfers to a fake account. The document was generated in minutes by an attacker. A lending officer funds a loan based on income documents that never existed. They looked real.

Visual inspection lost the arms race. AI produces forged documents faster than teams can examine them.

The shift required is fundamental. Stop asking "does this look right." Start asking "can we prove this came from a legitimate source."

What doesn't work anymore:
✘ Looking harder at the artefact.
✘ Checking metadata.
✘ Visual inspection by experts.
✘ Waiting to verify after approval.

The control that works:
✔ Verify origin at point of entry, not after loss.
✔ Use cryptographic proof tied to signing event.
✔ Make verification automatic.
✔ Apply this to KYC, vendor onboarding, contracts.

Detection fails because both detector and generator improve monthly. But provenance verification is deterministic. Either the file matches the original signing record or it doesn't.

Deloitte projects AI-enabled fraud losses in the US could reach $40 billion by 2027, up from $12.3 billion in 2023. Forged documents are a leading driver. That's from each fraudster becoming more productive.

Stop relying on appearance. Verify origin at intake.

Your payment system approved the transaction.
Your fraud system flagged it 4 minutes later.
That 4-minute gap just cost you real money — and it happens more often than most teams admit.
Here's the problem: in a lot of companies, fraud detection and payment processing run as two separate systems. They don't talk to each other in real time. So by the time fraud signals get reviewed, the payment has already gone through.
The result?
→ Fraud gets caught after the money moves, not before
 → Good customers get falsely declined because fraud scoring is working off stale or incomplete data
 → Support, risk, and payments teams are all looking at different versions of the "truth"
Here's the thing — the most valuable fraud signals (device fingerprint, transaction velocity, geolocation, behavioral patterns) are only powerful if they're evaluated at the exact moment of payment. Not 4 minutes later. Not in a nightly batch job.
If you're rethinking your fraud stack, don't start by adding another ML model.
Start by unifying your transaction and risk-scoring pipelines so fraud detection and payments are reading from the same real-time data.
The tech gets a lot easier once the data isn't fighting itself.
Is your fraud team seeing the same data as your payments team — in real time? Or are they still working off two different pictures?

Fraud detection and fraud investigation are closely connected, but they serve different purposes in insurance claims management.

#Fraud Detection

Fraud detection focuses on identifying #warning signs at an early stage. It uses #dataanalysis, rule based alerts, exception reports, predictive models and pattern monitoring to highlight claims that may require closer review.

Common indicators may include:

• Multiple #claims with similar #information
• Unusual claim frequency or timing
• Inconsistent #documents or #statements
• Claim patterns that differ from normal #customer behaviour
• Transactions that trigger predefined risk rules

Fraud Investigation

Fraud investigation begins after a claim has been flagged or a reasonable suspicion has emerged. It involves a detailed examination of facts, documents, evidence and circumstances to determine whether fraud has actually occurred.

The process may include:

• Reviewing policy and claim documents
• Interviewing claimants, witnesses and service providers
• Conducting field inquiries
• Validating the reported loss
• Collecting and preserving evidence
• Coordinating with #legal, #forensic or #technical experts

The key difference

Fraud detection identifies suspicion, while fraud investigation tests that suspicion through evidence.

A strong claims control framework requires both. Detection helps insurers identify potentially risky cases, while investigation supports informed decisions on whether to pay, reject, recover or escalate a claim.

Many organizations believe machine learning starts with data. It doesn’t. It starts with consistent decisions. Every predictive model learns from the choices people have already made. If those choices are inconsistent, incomplete, or poorly documented, the model simply reproduces those weaknesses at scale. The quality of an AI system is often limited long before a data scientist opens Python.

One of the most valuable questions an analytics consultant can ask isn’t:
“How accurate is your model?”
It’s:
“How consistently does your organization make this decision today?”
If experts disagree, the first project isn’t artificial intelligence. It’s operational clarity. Only after people agree on the decision should machines begin learning it. That’s why successful AI transformations rarely begin with neural networks or cloud infrastructure. They begin with something much less glamorous. Shared understanding.
Because before teaching machines to recognize fraud, organizations must first ensure that humans recognize it the same way.

When people hear about payment screening, they often use Fraud and Sanctions interchangeably.

But they are actually solving two very different problems.
Let's understand with a simple example. 👇

💳 Scenario
Imagine you receive a call from someone claiming to be your bank.
They convince you to transfer ₹50,000 to "secure" your account.
You make the payment.

1️⃣Fraud Check: "Is this payment suspicious?"
The payment is going to a normal bank account and a normal person.
But the transaction itself looks unusual because:
✅ It's larger than your typical transfers
✅ It's going to a new beneficiary
✅ You were tricked into initiating it

The bank's Fraud System asks:
"Could the customer be getting scammed?"

Fraud detection focuses on behavior and transaction patterns.

2️⃣Sanctions Check: "Are we allowed to pay this person?"
Now imagine the payment is being sent to a person or organization that appears on a government sanctions list.
Even if the payment is genuine and you willingly initiated it:
✅ No scam involved
✅ No suspicious activity
✅ Everything looks normal
The bank may still stop the payment because regulations prohibit doing business with that individual or organization.
Sanctions screening asks:
"Are we legally allowed to send money to this party?"

content:
When discussing regulatory strategy, one question comes up again and again:

“Can this device be cleared through the 510(k) pathway?” 

In reality, that question is often more complex than it sounds.

The question is whether the device meets the statutory requirements for a 510(k)—specifically, whether there is an appropriate predicate and whether substantial equivalence can be demonstrated.

In some cases, additional reference devices may also be useful to support comparisons of specific technological characteristics, but they do not replace the need for an appropriate predicate.

If those requirements cannot be met, a De Novo may be the appropriate pathway for a novel, low-to-moderate risk device.

The challenge is that it isn’t always obvious.

Technology, intended use, indications for use, risk profile, and available predicates all matter.

One of the most important jobs of a regulatory consultant isn’t predicting FDA’s decision—it’s helping clients understand the regulatory risks, prepare the strongest evidence package, and navigate the most likely regulatory pathway.

The right answer to the wrong version of a regulation is still wrong.

That sounds obvious.

Most software does not treat it that way.

Ask what a regulatory requirement says today and the answer may be straightforward.

Ask what that requirement said on the date a decision was made, a control was implemented, or a policy was approved, and the problem changes.

Now you need history.

Which version applied?

When did it become effective?

What changed?

What did it replace?

Which source supported the requirement at that point in time?

Regulatory truth is temporal.

And the useful unit is not the document.

It is the verified obligation, structured for machines and tied back to the source that created it.

That becomes even more important as AI starts answering questions people previously researched manually.

Retrieval cannot simply mean finding the most relevant paragraph.

It has to mean finding the right paragraph, from the right source, under the right version, at the right point in time.

Otherwise, you can produce a beautifully sourced answer that is still wrong.

This is why regulatory data needs to carry its own history.

Source.
Version.
Effective date.
Amendment.
Supersession.
Obligation.
Citation.

That is not metadata sitting beside the data.

It is part of the data itself.

For regulated financial institutions, knowing what the rule says matters.

For the technology companies serving them, it matters too.

Being able to reconstruct the regulatory state behind a decision is something else entirely.

A search box gives you an answer.

Verified regulatory data preserves what was true, when it was true.

- Patterns: Algorithms find trends in decades of market data.

Humans rely on meaning. We work with lived experience and emotion.

AI provides the numbers. You provide the judgment.
